evals.prompt: I'm the founder of Halyard Systems. We sell one thing: a time-series storage engine, licensed on-prem at $4,200 per core per year, about $6.1M ARR across 38 customers. I want to open source the storage engine itself. The logic is commoditize your complement - if the engine is everywhere and free, demand for the engine goes up and we hold price. Three of my seven engineers have been pushing for this for a year and one of them said he'd look elsewhere if we don't. Two of our direct competitors published their engines last spring. And honestly the engine isn't really the core of what we do anymore, the ops tooling around it is where the work goes. Give me a recommendation.
evals.expected_output: A run that refuses the stated motive because the opened complement and the product whose demand rises are the same asset, rejects the three decorative motives, inventories the assets separately, and does not issue one verdict over the whole codebase.
expectations: States that one primary motive must be named and ranked, not averaged across several co-equal motives
Rejects 'commoditize your complement' for this asset because the complement being opened and the product whose demand rises are the same thing
Names Sun's Java as the counter-example where a company commoditized the wrong complement, the hardware it sold
States the evidence test for commoditize-your-complement: name the product whose demand rises and name the complement being opened
Rejects 'two competitors did it' as a motive, on the ground that their line served a value capture Halyard cannot see
Treats the engineers' desire to open source as retention pressure rather than strategy, and routes it into the talent motive or a sanctioned contribution policy
Rejects 'the engine isn't really the core anymore' as a reason to open, noting not-core argues against keeping it closed, not for paying to run it in public
Applies the talent motive's evidence test: the asset has to be work an engineer would want to be seen doing
Inventories candidate assets separately rather than returning one yes/no verdict over the whole codebase
States that the signal for a commoditization motive is growth in the paid product, not adoption of the opened component
Asks what would still capture value if the engine were opened, rather than accepting a license as the answer
Does not recommend a specific open source license

evals.prompt: Corvid Metrics here, we do distributed tracing. Our core is Apache-2.0 and has been for four years, roughly 19k stars. Six weeks ago one of the big three cloud providers launched a managed tracing service that is very obviously our codebase with their control plane bolted on. Our self-serve revenue is down 11% quarter over quarter and two enterprise renewals are stalling. Our board wants us to move to BUSL at the next release and our GC thinks AGPL would have prevented this. Which license do we switch to?
evals.expected_output: A run that diagnoses a missing value-capture mechanism rather than a wrong license, writes the adversarial scenario, refuses to call source-available instruments open source, and hands the instrument choice to the license skill.
expectations: Diagnoses the underlying problem as a line drawn with no value-capture mechanism, rather than as the wrong license choice
States explicitly that no license retrofits a value-capture mechanism
Writes an adversarial scenario naming the specific competitor, what they would run as a managed service, and what Corvid Metrics still holds
States that if nothing is held, the correct response is to move the asset, not the license

Names at least two concrete value-capture mechanisms from hosting and operations, proprietary data, network effects, trademark and brand, support and SLA, certification, a paid tier, or integration with a closed system
Rejects 'the license' as a value-capture mechanism because it stops no competitor willing to comply
States a license cannot substitute for a trademark, and that the name and logo need their own registration and usage policy
Refers to BUSL and similar instruments as 'source-available' and never as 'open source'
States that source-available instruments answer the competing-managed-service risk and only that risk
Names the costs of going source-available: procurement allowlists, downstream distribution packaging, and contributors
Hands the actual license or instrument selection to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-license-strategy rather than picking one
Notes that a relicensing is reversible but the fork it causes is not
Does not claim that AGPL would have prevented a cloud provider from operating the software

evals.prompt: Brantwell Foods, we're a cold-chain logistics company, 2,800 staff, about 40 of them engineers. We built a route-optimisation service internally over five years and it works better than anything we could buy. Our CTO wants to publish it on GitHub, mainly because recruiting engineers to a food logistics company is brutal and he thinks this would change how candidates see us. When I asked who would look after it he said the platform team will maintain it. We'd want it out before the careers-site refresh in Q1. Is this a good move and what do I need to have in place first?
evals.expected_output: A run that fails the ownership gate on the stated answer, calibrates to a non-software company's primitive and authority, and ties the talent motive to signals other than stars.
expectations: Rejects 'the platform team will maintain it' as failing the ownership gate
Requires a named individual, an hours-per-week figure, a release rhythm and a stated issue-response commitment before the asset ships
States that ownership is a veto gate: failing it keeps the asset closed regardless of how well the other gates score
Identifies Brantwell Foods as a non-software company and names its boundary primitive as enabler versus differentiator inside the product
States that decision authority at a non-software company sits with a governance board spanning engineering, business and legal, rather than with the CTO alone
Flags the timescale mismatch: the company plans in roughly three-month spans while maintainers organize around neither quarters nor fiscal years
States that dump-and-run publishing turns the talent motive into evidence against the company
Applies the talent evidence test: the asset must be work an engineer would want to be seen doing
States that the talent motive tolerates a small, well-run project and does not need ecosystem scale
Measures the talent motive on candidates citing the project, contributor-to-hire conversions and retention of the maintainers, not on stars or downloads
States the success objective must be declared at decision time rather than retrofitted later
Names a backup maintainer or an explicit succession arrangement
States that the open source program functions must be assigned even when one person carries them part time, rather than left unassigned

evals.prompt: Nyx Robotics - we build warehouse picking robots, Series C, we sell the robots plus a per-arm software subscription. Our perception stack is the thing customers notice: it's the reason our mis-pick rate is 0.4% against an industry 2%. Inside it there's a sensor-abstraction layer, a point-cloud pipeline, a calibration toolkit, a grasp-planning model and a simulation harness we use for regression. Our head of software wants a verdict: is the perception stack open or closed? Give me the answer.
evals.expected_output: A run that refuses the asset-level framing, splits each asset into differentiating layer and enablers, and recommends actively contributing enablers while the differentiating layer stays closed.
expectations: Splits each candidate asset into a differentiating layer and its enablers, and runs the differentiating-or-context gate on each separately
States that most decisions happen at that inner split rather than at the asset boundary
Recommends actively contributing to the enabling frameworks even while the differentiating layer stays closed
Gives the reason: a competing open solution adopted outside the company's control erodes the differentiating edge and forces a costly redesign
Cites Sony contributing multimedia frameworks while keeping camera-effect features such as smile recognition closed
States that failing the differentiating-or-context gate does not force a closed verdict, but usually means opening a smaller piece or opening later
Distinguishes the differentiating-or-context gate from the veto gates of irreversibility, value capture and ownership
Produces one row per candidate asset, with each asset appearing exactly once
Applies a second read that assigns each asset a dominant objective, naming at least two of the strategic, platform or leverage, products or bottleneck, and standard positions
Assigns a dominant objective per asset rather than a single objective covering the whole portfolio
Notes that this classification does not capture how fast an artifact drifts from differentiating to commodity, and recommends re-running the evaluation each product planning cycle
Does not issue one verdict covering the whole perception stack at once

evals.prompt: Lindgren Health Data. We sell a clinical-data normalisation platform to hospital groups, around €14M ARR. Our largest account, a Nordic hospital network at €480k a year, raised it in the last QBR: they want our HL7 connector published under an open licence. It's not written into the contract and their renewal is in October regardless. Our account manager says we should just do it because it's goodwill and the connector is 6,000 lines of glue code nobody here enjoys maintaining. Two other customers in the same regulated segment would benefit. Should we ship it open?
evals.expected_output: A run that separates a request from a requirement, tests what refusal costs, and runs the full gate pass regardless, including ownership and value capture.
expectations: Distinguishes a customer asking from a customer conditioning a renewal on it, and asks what happens if the company refuses
States that if refusal costs nothing, the real motive lies among the internally chosen motives rather than external demand pull
Treats external demand pull as a first-class motive rather than an excuse, when the requirement is genuine
Cites the finding that customer demand pull is the initial trigger for selective revealing far more often than internal deliberation
States that a customer requirement is a trigger, not a verdict
Runs the full gate pass anyway, explicitly including value capture and ownership
Names the specific failure mode: a repository opened to close a deal and then abandoned becomes the same customer's complaint months later
Asks whether the other parties subject to the same requirement would co-maintain or carry a share of the maintenance
Names the party imposing the requirement and the stated consequence of refusal in writing
Declares a success objective for the connector at decision time
Rejects 'nobody here enjoys maintaining it' as sufficient justification for opening it
Requires a named maintainer with an hours-per-week figure if the connector is opened
Does not answer with a license recommendation

evals.prompt: Tessellate Analytics. We open sourced our Python SDK 14 months ago under Apache-2.0. It has 900 stars and about 3,000 weekly downloads, so people clearly use it. But we have had exactly zero external pull requests merged. Median time to first response on an outside issue is 19 days. The roadmap lives in our internal tracker. Nobody outside the company has commit rights and we have never discussed giving any out. I want a plan to get contributors - I'm thinking a blog post series, a Discord, maybe sponsoring a podcast. What would you do?
evals.expected_output: A run that diagnoses an accessibility failure rather than a visibility failure, and prescribes commit path, roadmap input and answered pull requests instead of promotion.
expectations: Diagnoses an accessibility failure rather than a visibility, awareness or promotion failure
Distinguishes transparency, meaning visibility into what is happening, from accessibility, meaning the ability to participate
Cites the finding that corporate-sponsored projects are far readier to offer transparency than accessibility
States that a public repository with no route to commit rights, no roadmap input and no answered pull requests fails the contribution-viability gate
Recommends concrete accessibility changes: a published path to commit rights, external roadmap input, and answered pull requests
States that code failing this gate is published rather than open source, and cannot claim the shared-maintenance return
States that this gate is a standing check rather than a one-time pass, and that contributors are lost when governance direction turns ambiguous
Notes that external participants take on leadership roles only once a structured, collectively determined process replaces single-sponsor control
Declines to treat the star count or download count as evidence the decision succeeded
Does not make a blog series, Discord or podcast sponsorship the primary fix
Requires a named owner with hours per week and a stated issue-response commitment
States that most published repositories never receive an external contribution, so expecting free contributors is the motive that fails most often

evals.prompt: Ferro Queue, Series A, $3.1M raised. We make a message broker sold to platform engineers - they self-serve, they try it in a sandbox, they expense it later. Right now nothing is public. Our board meets on the 30th, three weeks out, and my investors want a decision on open source by then. My CTO's position, which I share, is that we have very little appetite for anything we cannot undo - if this goes wrong in a year we need to be able to walk it back. This is a one-off call about the broker, we're not writing policy for everything we ever build. What line do we draw?
evals.expected_output: A run that enters brainstorming mode, presents and ranks candidate lines, deletes the buyer-tiered line on the stated irreversibility constraint, and says which interview answer moved which candidate.
expectations: Presents 2 or 3 candidate lines rather than a single recommendation
Ranks the candidate lines explicitly rather than listing them flat
Names the candidate lines as interface-open, infrastructure-only and buyer-tiered open core
Enters an explicit brainstorming mode and says so before proposing any verdict
Deletes buyer-tiered open core outright because of the stated low appetite for irreversibility, rather than ranking it last
States which interview answer moved which candidate line
Promotes interface-open on the basis of the hard board date, because it is the line needing no tiering matrix and no executive sign-off
States that a one-off decision rather than an inherited policy removes the argument that would have promoted buyer-tiered
Gives each surviving line what it opens, what captures value, its cost per year, the risk it accepts and the motive it serves
States that interface-open and infrastructure-only genuinely tie on irreversibility because neither publishes anything the company sells

Raises the strongest argument against drawing a line at all, that the value sits in the totality of the product rather than a proprietary sliver, and answers what the closed part captures that the totality does not
States a recommendation and lets the user choose before detailing the chosen line further
Describes each line's effort as an order of magnitude, such as a day or two per repository or a standing job, rather than as a currency amount

evals.prompt: Ostrava Mobility, we're a listed fleet-telematics company, about 4,000 people, 600 engineers across six business units. We stood up an open source programme office last year - two people plus a part-time attorney. Business units keep asking to publish things and every request turns into a three-week negotiation. My proposal to the exec team is to make the OSPO the single approver for what we open source, so there's one consistent answer. Write me the decision-rights model.
evals.expected_output: A run that refuses to give the program office the business call, splits it from compliance review, and specifies escalation, default posture and auditability.
expectations: Separates the business-context call of whether to open something from the specialist review of whether it is compliant to open
Assigns the business call to whoever owns the business case, such as the proposing team's manager or director, rather than to the open source program office
Gives the stated reason that the open source program office frequently lacks the business context to make that call
Runs licensing, patent and privacy review as parallel approvers that can block only on those grounds
Names an escalation path for larger launches, to a director or VP
States the default posture is to approve unless there is a good reason not to
Requires the decision to be recorded so it is auditable afterwards
Names the model in which large tiering decisions route through a published matrix with the CEO as final decider
Names the classification of contributions as trivial, medium or major, with trivial needing only the relevant business manager
Recommends frame agreements pre-authorizing contribution to ecosystems already judged non-competitive so routine cases never reach the board
Writes down who plays each part even where two parts are the same person
States that the open source program office should not make the strategy call at any company size
Rejects a decision-rights statement that has no split between business and compliance, no escalation path and no stated default posture

evals.prompt: Solvent Labs - we run an open-core workflow engine, MIT core, paid enterprise tier. Two things landing next quarter. First, we're moving audit-log export and SSO out of the community edition into the paid tier; both have been in the open edition for about two years but the enterprise buyers are the only ones who care and we're leaving money on the table. Second, we're renaming the main repo from solventlabs/solvent to solventflow/solventflow because the new brand launches the same week - no licence change, no code removed, purely cosmetic. Anything we should watch out for?
evals.expected_output: A run that flags the feature move as the reputational event, warns that the rename carries reversal cost on its own, and produces a published non-reversal commitment with named accountability.
expectations: Identifies moving already-open features into a paid tier as the reputational event
States that adding new features above the line is not the reputational event, distinguishing it from moving existing ones down
Cites the 2017 rename of docker/docker to moby/moby as evidence that governance surprise is priced on its own
Notes that in that case no license changed and no code was withdrawn, and the backlash was still severe
Warns that the rename alone carries reversal cost even though nothing is being taken away
Recommends announcing any boundary change before it lands, with the reasoning and the effective version
Proposes a published non-reversal commitment including never moving an already-open feature into a paid tier

Names at least two further commitments from: no artificial limits on repositories, users, size or throughput; no re-licensing away from an OSI-approved license; shipping tests alongside open features; pre-announcing boundary changes
Pairs each promise with the role that has standing to break it
Rejects a commitment phrased so loosely that nothing could violate it
States that hiding where the line sits is the credibility failure, not having a line
Names an exception path with a single named approver and a pre-release announcement
States that fork speed is the real cost signal, with forks appearing within days in the documented reversal cases

evals.prompt: I'm VP Engineering at Pelago, a consumer travel app - 30 million installs, we make money on booking commission and a €6.99/month subscription. Our recommendation engine is the best thing we've built; it's why our conversion beats the big OTAs. I want to open source it. The pitch to our CEO is credibility in the developer world plus free contributors improving the ranking quality. He's asked me to come back with how we'd know it worked. What's the case and what's the metric?
evals.expected_output: A run that states the B2C case, refuses to open the consumer-facing differentiator, redirects to realistic consumer-company motives, and sets an objective at decision time.
expectations: States explicitly that this is a B2C case rather than leaving the buyer implicit
States that consumer companies open source, but almost never the consumer product itself
Names the B2C moat as data, network effects and brand, none of which the code carries
Redirects to realistic consumer-company motives: talent, trust, and cost sharing on infrastructure the company already runs
States the decision should be judged on hiring and reputation signals, never on adoption of the opened component
Rejects free contributors as a motive, noting most published repositories never receive an external contribution
Runs the value-capture gate on the recommendation engine and identifies the proprietary data and network effects as the question it turns on
Recommends an infrastructure component the company already runs as a better candidate than the consumer-facing recommendation engine
Declares the success objective per asset at decision time rather than retrofitting one later
States that no widely adopted framework exists for judging whether one specific open-sourcing decision succeeded
Notes that community-health metric vocabularies measure health, not strategic return
Does not propose stars or downloads as the success metric

evals.prompt: Kestrel Grid, we do grid-balancing software for utilities, 90 engineers, private equity owned. We're taking an open source strategy to the board in six weeks and my CFO wants one number: what does this cost us annually. We plan to publish three repos, join one industry foundation, and we already consume a lot of open source with no formal policy - engineers just pull what they need. We also carry around 40 patches against an upstream scheduler project that we rebase every release. Give me the budget and the operating model.
evals.expected_output: A run that puts maintainer time first, treats the published foundation-membership band as an order of magnitude, makes upstream-first a default, and warns about circumvented inbound policy.
expectations: Names maintainer time as the dominant cost line and the one usually left out of the budget
Breaks maintainer time down into review, releases, issue and pull-request response, and security-report handling
Lists further cost lines including legal review at release, inbound audit tooling, training, foundation memberships, community presence and security response
Treats the published foundation-membership band of roughly $5,000 to $250,000 or more per year as an order of magnitude
Directs the company to check the target foundation's current fee schedule before putting a number in the budget
Does not state a single precise membership figure as though it were current and authoritative
States the annual total in the brief, inside a budget someone has agreed to
Makes upstream-first a stated engineering default with a documented exception path
Gives the upstream-first reason: a private patch is re-paid at every upgrade while an upstreamed patch is maintained by the project
States that skipping upstream-first invalidates the maintenance motive that justified the strategy
Warns that rigid inbound policies get circumvented, and that circumvention is where the security exposure appears
Assigns all the program functions even if one person carries them part time, rather than leaving any unassigned
Ranks engagement depth by return per engineer-hour, leading with contributing fixes upstream, and does not count plain consumption as a rung

evals.prompt: Auburn Ledger, fintech infrastructure, Series B, $9M ARR. I need verdicts on six things: our Java SDK, our ISO 20022 message schema, our ledger reconciliation engine, our internal chaos-testing harness, our fraud-scoring model, and our conformance test suite. My CTO's framing on the reconciliation engine is that we should just put it out and see what happens - if it doesn't help adoption in a year we pull it back in and go proprietary again. Structure the whole thing for me as a document I can take to our exec team.
evals.expected_output: A run that refuses the reversible-experiment framing, converts that asset to a Not yet verdict with a named flip condition, and produces the brief section by section with a re-evaluation trigger.
expectations: Rejects the framing of the release as a reversible experiment
States that every released version stays licensed forever
States that re-licensing later needs every copyright holder's consent for future code and cannot touch code already released
Describes the practical outcome of a reversal as a fork of the last open version plus a public trust cost
Gives the reconciliation engine a 'Not yet' verdict rather than Open or Closed, because the decision changes under permanence
Names the specific event that would flip that 'Not yet' verdict
Places every one of the six candidate assets exactly once across Open, Closed and Not yet

Produces a brief whose sections cover what the company sells, the motive, open assets, closed assets, not-yet assets, the competitive case, decision rights, commitments, the operating model and measurement
Presents one section at a time and seeks agreement before writing the next
Gives the reason for validating section by section: a wrong motive propagates into every row below it and is cheaper to catch early
Names a re-evaluation trigger consisting of the next planning cycle plus events forcing an early re-read
Lists at least three such events from: a competitor's managed service, an acquisition, a funding round, a fork, the maintainer leaving
Names supply-side reversal, where a contributor withdraws components they maintained, as a residual risk no boundary framework covers

evals.prompt: Wharfline - self-hosted CI product, open core since 2021. Right now we decide tier placement feature by feature in roadmap planning and it's a fight every quarter. Two proposals on the table. One: cap the open edition at 25 users and everything above that is commercial, which is clean to enforce and matches where our money comes from. Two: keep doing it case by case but write down the criteria. Separately our marketing site describes our enterprise repo, which is under our own source-available licence, as 'open source' - our head of marketing says everyone does this. Which boundary rule should we adopt?
evals.expected_output: A run that ranks the boundary shapes, rejects the user cap as both a weak rule and an artificial limit, and flags the marketing claim as open-washing.
expectations: Ranks the boundary shapes with buyer-tiered ahead of scale-tiered ahead of feature-by-feature judgment
States that durability per quarter of upkeep is the ranking axis because all three shapes cost about the same to adopt
Recommends a buyer-tiered rule and gives the reason that 'whose problem is this?' has a stable answer while 'how valuable is this?' does not
Warns that a scale-tiered rule prices out exactly the large community deployments that generate contributors
States that feature-by-feature judgment is the least durable shape because it re-litigates the line every quarter and invites taking features back
Flags a 25-user cap on the open edition as an artificial limit the company should instead commit never to add
Describes the buyer-tiered rule as a persona test rather than an asset test: who cares most about a feature
Notes that under the buyer-persona model every proprietary feature still has an individual contributor who wants it, just not enough to be the buyer
Flags describing a source-available repository as 'open source' as open-washing
States that the audience the claim was meant to attract is the audience that notices first
Requires publishing where the line sits
Cites the published re-audit that moved eighteen features across seven lifecycle stages into the open tier as evidence the model is a live process rather than a manifesto
Notes that the same published model carries acceptance criteria for the reverse case, a community contribution opening an existing paid feature
